::: proof
We write the proof with integrals;
for a probability mass function, replace each integral with a sum.
Because the support does not depend on $\theta$,
we can differentiate under the integral sign.

The derivative of the density with respect to $\theta$ is

$$
\ba
\deriv{\theta} f(y; \theta, \phi)
&= f(y; \theta, \phi)
\deriv{\theta}\sb{\frac{y\theta - b(\theta)}{\phi} + c(y, \phi)}
&& \text{(chain rule for the exponential)}
\\ &= f(y; \theta, \phi) \frac{y - b'(\theta)}{\phi}
&& \text{(differentiate term by term)}
\ea
$$

Every density integrates to 1, for every value of $\theta$,
so differentiating that identity once gives the mean:

$$
\ba
0 &= \deriv{\theta} \int f(y; \theta, \phi)\, dy
&& \text{(derivative of the constant 1)}
\\ &= \int \deriv{\theta} f(y; \theta, \phi)\, dy
&& \text{(differentiate under the integral)}
\\ &= \int \frac{y - b'(\theta)}{\phi} f(y; \theta, \phi)\, dy
&& \text{(derivative of the density)}
\\ &= \frac{\E{Y} - b'(\theta)}{\phi}
&& \text{(definition of expectation, and } \textstyle\int f = 1\text{)}
\ea
$$

Multiplying both sides by $\phi > 0$ gives $\E{Y} = b'(\theta)$.

{{< slidebreak >}}

Differentiating the same identity a second time gives the variance:

$$
\ba
0 &= \deriv{\theta} \int \frac{y - b'(\theta)}{\phi} f(y; \theta, \phi)\, dy
&& \text{(derivative of the constant 0)}
\\ &= \int \sb{-\frac{b''(\theta)}{\phi} f(y; \theta, \phi)
+ \frac{y - b'(\theta)}{\phi} \deriv{\theta} f(y; \theta, \phi)} dy
&& \text{(product rule)}
\\ &= \int \sb{-\frac{b''(\theta)}{\phi}
+ \frac{\paren{y - b'(\theta)}^2}{\phi^2}} f(y; \theta, \phi)\, dy
&& \text{(derivative of the density)}
\\ &= -\frac{b''(\theta)}{\phi} + \frac{\E{\paren{Y - b'(\theta)}^2}}{\phi^2}
&& \text{(definition of expectation, and } \textstyle\int f = 1\text{)}
\\ &= -\frac{b''(\theta)}{\phi} + \frac{\Varf{Y}}{\phi^2}
&& \text{(} b'(\theta) = \E{Y}\text{, so this is the variance)}
\ea
$$

Multiplying both sides by $\phi^2$ and rearranging gives
$\Varf{Y} = \phi\, b''(\theta)$.
:::
